title: Octopus: Experiences with a Hybrid Event-Driven Architecture for Distributed Scientific Computing
problem: Scientific computing applications must efficiently handle events generated from many distributed sources across HPC systems, cloud infrastructure, and edge devices, requiring reliable communication, processing organization, and secure access control.
motivation: Event-driven architecture enables resilient applications to effectively manage and process events from heterogeneous distributed research infrastructures spanning the compute continuum.
method: Octopus links event sources and processors across edge devices, cloud data centers, and supercomputers by routing all events through cloud-hosted brokers—central hubs that organize and forward them. The system automatically activates responses to specific events, enforces detailed permission rules about what each component can access, and adjusts computing resources based on how many events arrive. When parts of the network fail, the system finds alternate routes so events still reach their destinations.
key_novelty: A unified system for routing events (messages about things happening) across the full range of scientific computing infrastructure—from edge devices to cloud systems to supercomputers.
contributions: Octopus hybrid event-driven architecture supporting scientific computing across cloud and edge resources
High-availability Trigger mechanisms for automatic event processing with fine-grained access control
Identification of event-driven architecture requirements in self-driving laboratories, data automation, online scheduling, epidemic modeling, and workflow management
Demonstrated performance of 4.2M events/sec production and 9.6M events/sec consumption from distributed clients
limitations: Limitations and scalability boundaries under specific deployment scenarios are not discussed.
primary_theme: hybrid event-driven infrastructure for distributed scientific computing
